lines: A hundred and twenty two degrees Fahrenheit. Fifty degrees Celsius.
It sounds impossible. It isn't.
Four states have already gone past it. California, Arizona, Nevada and New Mexico.
Death Valley hit a hundred and thirty four, back in nineteen thirteen.
And in twenty twenty one, a heat wave pushed Washington State to a hundred and twenty.
A state where a lot of people never needed air conditioning.
Washington's health department counted a hundred and twelve heat deaths.
So here's the experiment. One week. A hundred and twenty two degrees. In every state at once.
Which state breaks first?
We used official numbers for all fifty states.
In heat like that, one thing decides who's in danger. Can you cool your home?
So we ranked every state by the share of homes with no air conditioning at all. Not even a window unit.
And we looked at one more thing. How hot each state has ever been.
Because 11 states have never even reached a hundred and ten.
Their houses, their roads and their power lines were never built for this.
Part one. The states that stay cool.
In 13 states, at least ninety five percent of homes have air conditioning.
Florida, 96 percent. Texas, 95.
No surprise there. They live with heat every summer.
But here's one that is a surprise.
Iowa. 97 percent of homes have air conditioning.
That's more than Arizona, at 94.
Iowa's record high is 118 degrees. Midwest summers are humid and brutal, and people there learned that a long time ago.
Illinois and New Jersey are at 96 percent. Delaware, 97.
In these states, a week at a hundred and twenty two would be miserable. But most people could close the door and turn on the AC.
Part two. The biggest number.
Across the whole country, about 14 million homes have no air conditioning.
And one state has more of them than anywhere else. By far.
California. Only 28 percent of homes have no AC. That doesn't sound like much.
But California is huge. That's 3.64 million homes.
More homes than the entire state of Washington has, with or without AC.
Along much of the coast, people never needed it. The ocean did the cooling for free.
New York has about 920 thousand homes with no AC. And of the ones that have it, most are window units.
Only 29 percent of New York homes have central air.
Part three. The top ten. These are the states that break first.
Number ten. New Hampshire. 22 percent of homes with no AC.
Number nine. Oregon. 24 percent. And Oregon already got a taste of this, in twenty twenty one.
Number eight. California, with the most homes at risk.
Number seven. Wyoming. 29 percent.
Number six. Maine. 30 percent. Its record high is a hundred and five.
Number five. Vermont. 33 percent. And only 7 percent of homes have central air.
Number four. Montana. 35 percent.
Number three. Hawaii. 43 percent. The trade winds have done the job for generations. Its record is just a hundred.
Number two. Washington. 47 percent. Almost half the state.
The state that already saw a hundred and twenty, and lost a hundred and twelve people.
And the state that breaks first.
Alaska. 93 percent of homes have no air conditioning.
Alaska's record high is exactly one hundred degrees, set at Fort Yukon in nineteen fifteen.
A hundred and twenty two would beat that record by twenty two degrees. In a state built to keep heat in, not out.
Part four. The pattern.
Here's every state. Across the bottom, its hottest day ever. Up the side, the share of homes with AC.
The states that have felt real heat bought air conditioning. The ones that never did, didn't.
That made sense for a hundred years.
But look at where the new records are being set.
Colorado in twenty nineteen. Oregon, Washington and Utah in twenty twenty one.
The heat is moving to the places that are least ready for it.
So which state breaks first? Alaska. Then Washington. Then Hawaii.
And the state with the most people at risk is California.
Does your home have air conditioning? And where do you live? Tell us in the comments.
And subscribe. Next week, another stress test for all fifty states.
